meta.title: Who really said "They Haven't Done Anything to My Book. It's Right There on the Shelf"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: James M. Cain, to the New York Times Book Review in March 1969. Not Raymond Chandler — that credit starts with William S. Burroughs in 1991.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'They Haven't Done Anything to My Book. It's Right There on the Shelf'?
meta.ogDescription: James M. Cain said it to the New York Times Book Review in March 1969. The Raymond Chandler version is a 1991 mix-up.

answer.label: Spoken by
answer.authorDates: 1892–1977 · American novelist and journalist — The Postman Always Rings Twice, Double Indemnity, Mildred Pierce
answer.sourceLine: Cain said it to the critic John Leonard, who visited him at home in Hyattsville, Maryland, for a piece in the New York Times Book Review of 2 March 1969. Quote Investigator ↗ transcribes the passage and names that article — “The Wish of James M. Cain”, quote page BR2, column 3 — as the earliest known appearance. Cain liked the answer enough to give it again, word for word, to The Paris Review eight years later.
answer.confidenceText: A specific, dated, paginated first appearance, with the speaker’s own words transcribed.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: The New York Times, Book Review section, 2 March 1969, p. BR2, col. 3
To The Paris Review, interviewed 7 January 1977, published 1978

source.excerpt: There are some foods some people just don’t like. I just don’t like movies. People tell me, don’t you care what they’ve done to your book? I tell them, they haven’t done anything to my book. It’s right there on the shelf. They paid me and that’s the end of it.
trail: Quote Investigator’s investigation ↗ concludes: “based on current evidence this saying should be credited to James M. Cain”, and “There is no substantive support for ascribing the quotation to Chandler.”

The earliest citation QI gives is 1969 March 2, New York Times, Section: Book Review, The Wish of James M. Cain by John Leonard, Quote Page BR2, Column 3 (consulted via ProQuest, and located by the researcher Bill Mullins). We have not seen the newspaper page ourselves; the transcription above is QI’s.

QI corroborates the wording twice over: a 1974 book, Graham Greene: The Films of His Fiction, quotes Cain in phrasing that “matched the version in the New York Times”; and in the Paris Review interview of 7 January 1977 Cain gave “the exact same sequence of six sentences”.

QI also traces the wrong credit: William S. Burroughs attached the anecdote to Raymond Chandler in a September 1991 introduction, and David Cronenberg (1992) and Alan Moore (2001) followed him. QI calls that ascription “caused by confusion and… mistaken” ↗.
source.excerptNote: Cain’s words as Quote Investigator ↗ transcribes them from the 1969 New York Times Book Review piece. The headline wording people search for — title-cased, two sentences — is a compression of the middle of this passage.

source.rightsNote: The words were spoken in 1969 and first printed in The New York Times Book Review of 2 March 1969. Nothing published in the United States from 1931 onward is public domain on age alone, so both that article and the Paris Review interview that repeats the passage are in copyright.

author.name: James M. Cain
author.heading: About James M. Cain
author.bio: James M. Cain (1 July 1892 – 27 October 1977) wrote the hard, fast crime novels that Hollywood turned into some of the defining films of the 1940s: The Postman Always Rings Twice, Double Indemnity, Mildred Pierce. He barely watched them. John Leonard reported in the New York Times in 1969 that Cain had seen only two of the films made from his books, and his standing answer to anyone who wanted him to be upset about it is the line on this page.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: The anecdote is good enough that it keeps getting reassigned to whichever novelist the teller has in mind. Only one of them is documented saying it.

items.why: The Chandler version starts with William S. Burroughs’s September 1991 introduction to Everything Is Permitted: The Making of Naked Lunch, twenty-two years after Cain is on record saying it. QI ↗ finds “no substantive support” for it, and judges the ascription a confusion — helped along by the fact that Chandler co-wrote the screenplay of Cain’s Double Indemnity.
Both retold it as a Chandler story, following Burroughs — Cronenberg at a Naked Lunch screening, Moore in an A.V. Club interview, per QI’s citations ↗.

A 2010 magazine piece QI quotes ↗ names the author “variously identified as William Faulkner, Raymond Chandler, and James M. Cain”; a separate 2002 interview tells it about Elmore Leonard. Neither has a citation behind it.
King has retold the anecdote at least twice — a 2006 Powell’s interview and a 2013 letter about Under the Dome — and both times he credited Cain, per QI ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: The line is Cain’s, said to a New York Times interviewer in 1969 and repeated unchanged to The Paris Review in 1977. QI’s trail ↗ is the account to read.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Cain had the most adapted body of work in American crime fiction and almost no interest in the adaptations. The remark is not a complaint about Hollywood — it is a refusal to be recruited into one. The reporter arrives with the grievance pre-packaged; Cain declines it and points at a shelf.
The last sentence is the one people drop, and it is the bluntest: They paid me and that’s the end of it. This is a working writer’s answer, not an aesthete’s.
detailsBody: It has become the standard thing for an author to say when a film of their book disappoints, which is why it has been handed to so many of them. Owen Sheers used a version of it in 2011; Larry Niven made the same point in 2003. The durable part is the logic: a film is a separate object, and it cannot reach back and alter the book.
context.pull: The book is a physical object on a shelf. Whatever the film did, it did somewhere else.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator concludes the saying should be credited to James M. Cain and that there is no substantive support for ascribing it to Raymond Chandler.

QI's earliest citation is 1969 March 2, New York Times, Book Review section, 'The Wish of James M. Cain' by John Leonard, Quote Page BR2, Column 3, located by Bill Mullins, and QI transcribes Cain's words including 'they haven't done anything to my book. It's right there on the shelf. They paid me and that's the end of it.'

QI records that Cain repeated the identical six-sentence answer in a Paris Review interview conducted 7 January 1977 and published in 1978, and that a 1974 book, Graham Greene: The Films of His Fiction, quoted phrasing matching the New York Times version.

QI traces the Raymond Chandler misattribution to William S. Burroughs's September 1991 introduction to 'Everything Is Permitted: The Making of Naked Lunch', followed by David Cronenberg in 1992 and Alan Moore in 2001, and records Stephen King crediting Cain in 2006 and 2013.
James M. Cain was an American novelist and journalist, born 1 July 1892 and died 27 October 1977.
